name: Nikhil Reyes

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or any government. What you tell me stays confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal week at university so far.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm in electronic engineering, so it's circuits, signals and a lot of soldering in the lab, which I enjoy. I live at home in a small town and commute forty minutes by train, because my parents run a corner shop and I help there in the evenings and on Saturdays. I stock shelves, do the till and handle the lottery machine. It's a long day, but I like being useful to my family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's what I thought. A lot of fuss over a clever tool. In the shop, our till system has been the same for years, and customers still want to chat to a person. I'd tell my cousins that working hard and learning a trade still pays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's reassuring for my degree and my family's shop. My worry is more ordinary: my grades are average, the shop's margins are thin, and big supermarkets keep opening nearby. I'd want a job after graduating that gives me stable pay, so I can help my parents.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as before. Study, help in the shop, keep costs low. I'd ask the careers service about a placement with a company that makes electronics or power equipment, and I'd keep the Saturday till shifts, because they're how I pay my train fare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine. I'm tired from the commute, but nothing new is pressing on me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned supermarkets opening nearby. How much does that worry you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A fair bit. A new supermarket opened on the bypass last spring, and our sales dropped about a tenth. My dad says we'll manage, but I can see him checking the figures at night.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take over the shop one day?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe, if it still makes sense. My parents would like that. But I'd want an engineering job first, so I could keep the shop going or help them close it with dignity.

say: It's a lot of fuss over a clever **tool**, and customers still want a person.
Working hard and learning a **trade** still pays.
think: My degree and the shop look safe, but **supermarkets** keep opening nearby.
I want stable **pay** so I can help my parents.
do: **Keep** helping in the shop and keep costs low.
Ask the careers service for a **placement** with an electronics or power firm.
feel: **Tired** from the commute, but nothing new presses on me.
S0.quote: A new supermarket opened on the bypass last spring, and our sales dropped about a tenth.
fieldNote: His **worry** is the shop's falling sales, not AI.
He treats the shop as a **duty** and a possible future.
His **steady** approach shows in wanting an engineering job first, then deciding.

steps.text: Keep working the till on Saturdays and weeknights
Ask the careers service about electronics placements
Check the shop's weekly figures with Dad

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's real, and the shop and the family need to think about it. I'd tell my cousins that offices will feel it first, and anything done on a screen. I'd say engineering will need people who can do both, the thinking and the hands-on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'm somewhat protected in my field, because electronics means real boards and real equipment. But design software will do more of the checking, and juniors might get squeezed. The shop's the bigger worry: supermarkets with AI stock systems can cut prices, and we can't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start using the AI tools in my circuit design course, since they're becoming normal. I'd practise at the lab bench, because hands-on skill will be worth more. And I'd help my parents set up a simple stock list or ordering tool, if one is cheap and proven.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Concerned, but not scared. Some things will change, some won't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would a stock tool help the shop?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We waste milk and bread because we guess wrong. If a tool says order twelve, not twenty, we save money every week. I'd test it for a month before telling Dad it's worth it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does your father say about AI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He says it's for the big boys. But he would use anything that saves money. If I show him a result, he'll listen. He doesn't like being told, but he likes proof.

say: Offices and **screen work** will feel it first.
Engineering will need people who can do both **thinking and hands-on**.
think: Electronics is partly protected, but **design checking** may squeeze juniors.
Supermarkets with AI stock systems can cut **prices**, and we can't.
do: Use the **AI tools** in my circuit design course and practise at the lab bench.
Set up a simple **stock list** for the shop if one is cheap and proven.
feel: **Concerned** but not scared, since some things will change and some won't.
S1.quote: We waste milk and bread because we guess wrong. If a tool says order twelve, not twenty, we save money every week.
fieldNote: He sees the AI change as a **shop problem** as much as a degree problem.
He will test a tool for a month before **proving** it to his dad.
His **steady** adaptability shows in trying tools once they're normal.

steps.text: Test a free stock ordering tool for the shop for a month
Use the AI features in circuit design coursework
Spend extra hours at the lab bench each week

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we should be careful and look after our own people. I'd tell my family that we should keep our savings and not take on debt. I'd say it's not right that a handful of companies could decide what happens to millions of workers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be worried sick. By 2028 I'd be in second year, and a lot of my field could be done by software. The shop would also be hit, since prices would fall and big chains would use robots and automation. By 2031 robots do hands-on work, which would reach stocking and delivery.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay in the degree for now and save everything I can. I'd speak with my parents about the shop's future and whether to sell it while it still has value. I'd look at a trade in electrical maintenance as a backup, because people will need that done for a while.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Heavy. I'd keep going, but with a stone in my stomach.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would your parents react to selling the shop?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Dad would refuse at first. He built it up himself. But Mum is practical and she'd listen if I laid out the figures. They'd probably want to keep going until it was clear we had no choice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you give up first, to save?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The train season ticket, by switching to a cheaper bus. And I'd stop buying parts for my own projects. I'd keep the lab fees, because the degree is still the best card I have.

say: Keep our **savings**, take on no debt and look after our own people.
A handful of companies shouldn't decide what happens to **millions** of workers.
think: By 2028 a lot of my field could be done by **software**.
The **shop** would be hit by falling prices and chains using robots.
do: **Save** everything I can and talk with my parents about the shop's future.
Look at **electrical maintenance** as a backup trade.
feel: **Heavy**, like a stone in my stomach, but I'd keep going.
S2.quote: Dad would refuse at first. He built it up himself. But Mum is practical and she'd listen if I laid out the figures.
fieldNote: The **shop and degree** are hit at once, so the mood is high.
He would lead the **family** conversation with figures.
He holds on to the **degree** as his best card.

steps.text: Show Mum and Dad the shop's figures and sale options
Switch from the train season ticket to a cheaper bus
Look into electrical maintenance courses as a backup
Save every shop wage into a separate account

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to make a plan, and families should sit down and do that. I'd tell the family that the shop should be run carefully, and we shouldn't borrow. I'd also say the next few years are a good time to learn a real skill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd feel some pressure but not despair. I'd finish my degree in 2029, then face AGI in 2031. Robots arrive about 2034, so hands-on electronics and maintenance might last longer. I'd aim for the practical side of engineering.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the degree and spend summers on placements in manufacturing or power. I'd keep helping in the shop, and set up a basic online order system so it could survive. I'd save toward a small deposit, and add a trade qualification if I can get it cheaply.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Cautious. It's a mix of nerves and a plan, which I can live with.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if the shop had to close in year three?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd move for work, probably to a bigger town, and help my parents find a smaller place. I'd want to be earning enough to cover part of their rent. It would be hard, but they'd understand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does your plan depend on a good grade?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A little, but placements matter more. A firm cares if you can fix a board and turn up. I'd make sure to be that person.

say: Five years is enough to make a **plan**, and families should sit down and do that.
The shop should be **run carefully** with no borrowing.
think: I'd finish in 2029, then face **AGI** in 2031.
Hands-on electronics and **maintenance** might last until about 2034.
do: Spend summers on **placements** in manufacturing or power.
Set up a basic **online order** system so the shop can survive.
feel: **Cautious**, a mix of nerves and a plan that I can live with.
S3.quote: A firm cares if you can fix a board and turn up. I'd make sure to be that person.
fieldNote: He plans around **practical skill**, in line with traditional values.
The shop could force a **move**, and he has already thought about it.

steps.text: Complete summer placements in manufacturing or power firms
Set up a basic online ordering page for the shop
Save toward a deposit and an electrical trade ticket

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a decent runway, and I'd tell people to keep calm and keep working. I'd tell the family we can adapt the shop over time. I'd say it's the right moment to learn skills that last, like fixing things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd feel quite relaxed. By 2036 I'd be 28, with a degree, a few years of work and savings. The shop might have changed, or my parents might have retired. Robots arrive around 2039, and electronics fixing would be among the later things to change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the degree and take a job with a company that makes or maintains equipment. I'd gradually bring in new tools at the shop, with proof they work. I'd save for a flat, and put something aside for my parents' retirement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fairly settled. A long road, but a clear one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want to change about your situation in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want the shop to be less of a worry for my parents. If it could run with fewer hours, they'd have more life outside it. That's my real hope for the next ten years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How is this different from the 2031 picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Time. In five years I'd be rushing, and in ten I can try things and fix mistakes. That's a big difference when money is tight.

say: Ten years is a decent runway, so **keep calm** and keep working.
We can **adapt** the shop over time.
think: By 2036 I'd be 28 with a **degree**, work experience and savings.
Electronics fixing would be among the **later** things to change.
do: **Finish** the degree and take a job with an equipment maker.
**Bring in** new shop tools gradually, with proof that they work.
feel: Fairly **settled**, on a long but clear road.
S4.quote: In five years I'd be rushing, and in ten I can try things and fix mistakes. That's a big difference when money is tight.
fieldNote: His hope is that the **shop** gives his parents more life outside it.
He compares the speed of the two worlds in terms of **mistakes**, a steady attitude.
Money is **tight** and still shapes the mood.

steps.text: Take a graduate job maintaining electronic equipment
Bring a proven stock tool into the shop step by step
Put money aside for my parents' retirement

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, because the shop and my degree would be hit together and I'd have no time. What would help is real support for small family shops, plus training places that lead to actual jobs. And someone being honest with families about what's coming.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask what the shop means to me. The shop is where I learned that you show up every day, and treat people properly. Whatever the machines do, I don't want to lose that.

headlineQuote: The shop is where I learned that you show up every day, and treat people properly. Whatever the machines do, I don't want to lose that.
portrait: Nikhil is 18, studies **electronic engineering** and commutes from a small town where his parents run a corner shop.
He is traditional, family-minded and **steady**, trying tools once they're proven and checking numbers with his dad.
His worries are the shop's falling sales and his own **first job**, more than the technology itself.
He moves from uneasy to **alarmed** if AGI arrives by 2028, with the shop and degree hit together.
biggestWorry: The **2028** picture worries him most, since the shop and his degree are hit together.
whatWouldHelp: Real support for **small family shops** and training that leads to actual jobs.
**Honest** information for families about what is coming.
